extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (trademark attorneys), OED staff, and counsel for trademark applicants (including U.S. counsel for foreign-domiciled clients)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing practitioner conduct when prosecuting trademark applications before the USPTO, with emphasis on signature rules, supervision, candor, competence, and the rules and consequences for exclusion on consent under the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct and related statutes/regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature requirements for trademark filings
rubrics_metrics.description: All documents must be personally signed or bear an electronic signature that was personally entered by the named signatory (TMEP § 611.01(c); 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a)(1), (c)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The TMEP states unambiguously that another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, secretary) may not sign or enter the name of an attorney or other authorized signatory. Impermissible signatures on filings compromise the integrity of the federal trademark registration process. Examples on the record: DIRECT signature method (computer used to sign is also the computer used to file) and H-SIGN (printed and pen-and-ink signatures). TEAS data showing filing location may be relevant to assessing where signing/filing occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must provide competent representation, which includes ensuring trademark applications comply with USPTO signature rules and other procedural requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence examples from the Order: do not file applications with impermissible applicant signatures; contact applicants to confirm they signed declarations; establish measures to ensure associated foreign companies comply with signature rules; prevent misuse of practitioner credentials; review filing receipts to verify filed documents were properly signed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order cites failure modes constituting lack of diligence: filing improperly signed applications, failing to contact applicants to confirm signatures, failing to implement measures to ensure compliance by referring entities, failing to prevent use of credentials for filings, and failing to review filing receipts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication and explanation to permit informed client decisions (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific duty: explain actual or potential adverse consequences of not complying with USPTO trademark signature rules — for example, whether electronic signing by someone other than the named signatory jeopardizes clients' intellectual property rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor to the tribunal (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.303(a)(1) and (a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not knowingly make false statements or fail to disclose material facts to the tribunal/Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: knowingly filing impermissibly signed trademark applications and failing to inform USPTO Trademark Operations about impermissibly signed applications and possible remedial measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.503(a) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must reasonably supervise non-practitioner assistants to ensure compliance with USPTO rules and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to supervise associated foreign companies that prepare, sign, or file trademark documents may violate these supervisory duties. The Order cites failure to make reasonable efforts to ensure foreign companies complied with USPTO signature rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assisting unauthorized practice of law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not assist others in the unauthorized practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to supervise foreign companies so they impermissibly prepared, signed, and filed responses to Office actions can amount to assisting unauthorized practice of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing impermissibly signed trademark applications that appeared to be signed by the applicants when they were not is cited as an example of such misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must avoid conduct prejudicial to the administration of the USPTO trademark registration system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impermissibly signed filings that negatively affect the integrity of the federal trademark registration process are prejudicial to administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other conduct reflecting adversely on fitness (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must avoid other conduct that adversely reflects on a practitioner's honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order treats certain acts/omissions in representation and in dealings with referring entities as potentially falling within this catch‑all provision if not covered by the specifically enumerated rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to conduct reasonable factual inquiry (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an obligation to conduct a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances in support of factual assertions made in trademark documents presented to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order cites § 11.18 in the context of ensuring signatures and statements in filings are supported by reasonable inquiry — practitioners should verify authenticity of applicant-signed declarations received via third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation to know applicable laws, rules, regulations, and guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners representing applicants, registrants, or others before the USPTO are reasonably expected to know the laws, rules, regulations, procedures, and relevant USPTO guidance (including the TMEP) applicable to their representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order emphasizes readily available USPTO materials (www.uspto.gov/trademarks, TMEP) and cites multiple prior disciplinary orders where failure to comply with signature rules or supervisory obligations led to discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature method definitions and evidentiary relevance (DIRECT and H-SIGN)
rubrics_metrics.description: DIRECT signature method: the computer used to sign the declaration is also the computer used to file the application. H-SIGN: the application including the declaration was printed and signed with pen-and-ink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order uses TEAS capture data (showing filing location) and signature method metadata to assess whether signatures were properly obtained and who actually signed/processed documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Resignation / Exclusion on Consent requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.27 and related)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Affidavit of Resignation seeking exclusion on consent must meet regulatory requirements and be voluntarily and knowingly rendered; the OED Director may present a disciplinary complaint and the Director of the USPTO may approve the affidavit leading to exclusion on consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the Respondent's affidavit: consent is freely and voluntarily rendered; respondent is aware under 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.27, 11.59, 11.60 of legal/factual consequences; respondent acknowledges that upon reinstatement application under § 11.60 the OED Director will conclusively presume the complaint allegations are true and that the respondent could not have successfully defended against them. The Director has authority under 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32 and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19 and 11.27 to approve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and conditions of exclusion on consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Approval of an Affidavit of Resignation results in exclusion on consent from practice before the Office in trademark and other non-patent matters, effective as ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order directs compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 and requires compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 upon any request for reinstatement (including the presumption described above). The Order also directs publication of the Final Order in the OED FOIA Reading Room and a materially consistent notice in the Official Gazette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and public notice requirements for disciplinary actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order in the OED FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the sample notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order contains a model notice of exclusion on consent summarizing the facts, the number of applications involved, associated referring entities, and the respondent's acknowledgement regarding reinstatement presumptions. Decisions are posted at https://foiadocuments.uspto.gov/oed.
